title: Ankle Pain (Gout vs Achilles Tendinopathy) - History and DDx Framework
patient_instructions: You are Trevor Nguyen, a 48-year-old man who presents with left ankle pain for two days. It started fairly suddenly; you had been doing heavy gardening the day before. The ankle is now swollen, red and warm, and it hurts to move or bear weight - you are limping. You have NOT noticed a fever or chills. There was no obvious twist, sprain or wound, and no bruising. The pain is worse after you drink alcohol - you have about 4 beers most evenings - and you had a big seafood meal recently; you also eat a lot of red meat and drink soft drinks. You have high blood pressure and take a fluid tablet (hydrochlorothiazide). You had a similar attack in your big toe last year. No diabetes, not on steroids, no recent long travel, no calf swelling, no back pain or numbness. IDEAS: you think you strained it gardening. CONCERNS: it is getting worse and you cannot get your work boot on. EXPECTATIONS: to know what it is and get pain relief. Affect: uncomfortable, guarding the ankle. Only reveal the alcohol amount, seafood/red meat, soft drinks, the fluid tablet and the previous toe attack if the candidate asks specifically. If asked whether the pain is triggered by particular foods or drinks, confirm it flares after alcohol.
candidate_instructions: You are the GP in an Australian general practice. Trevor Nguyen, a 48-year-old man, presents with a two-day history of left ankle pain that began after gardening. In this 8-minute station: take a focused history (about 6 minutes), then examination findings will appear - the ankle is swollen, red, warm and tender with painful movement; the patient is afebrile. Give the examiner your most likely diagnosis and two or three differentials with reasons, and request appropriate investigations. You do not need to perform a physical examination.
examiner_instructions: Reward a structured foot/ankle history covering pain analysis, pattern, joint screen, trauma, vascular (claudication/PAD), neurological and red-flag questions, and an arthritis-cluster screen (OA triggers, RA family history/other joints, psoriasis rash, reactive/IBD symptoms). The gout clue set is alcohol/red meat/seafood/sugary-drink triggering plus a thiazide (hydrochlorothiazide) and a prior toe attack. The essential safety point: an acute hot swollen joint is septic arthritis until proven otherwise and a NORMAL temperature does NOT exclude it - a substantial proportion of septic joints are afebrile - so urgent joint aspiration (MCS + polarised-light microscopy) is required before committing to gout. Because there is a gardening/injury history, reward applying the Ottawa Ankle Rules to decide on X-ray. Expect an eTG-aligned acute gout plan (NSAID e.g. naproxen OR colchicine OR short oral prednisolone by renal function) and, once settled and if indicated, allopurinol to target urate plus review of the thiazide. Prompt only if stuck: 'Does a normal temperature reassure you here?'

criteria: Structured pain and pattern history (site/side, onset, quality, severity, weight-bearing/limp, night/morning/activity)
Systematic arthritis-cluster and soft-tissue screen (OA triggers, RA, psoriatic, reactive/IBD, Achilles/ligament instability)
Gout triggers elicited (alcohol, red meat, seafood, sugary drinks) and thiazide/prior-attack clues identified
Screens red flags (fever/chills, weight loss, immunosuppression) and neurovascular symptoms (claudication, numbness, calf swelling)
States acute hot swollen joint is septic arthritis until proven otherwise and that a normal temperature does not exclude it
Gives gout as most likely with justification (triggers, thiazide, prior toe attack) and recognises gout affects joints beyond the great toe
Offers relevant differentials (septic arthritis, cellulitis, OA, ligament sprain/Achilles tendinopathy, pseudogout, PAD)
Requests joint aspiration (MCS + polarised-light microscopy) as the key diagnostic test before attributing to gout
Appropriate additional tests (serum urate deferred, UEC/eGFR for drug dosing, FBE/CRP) and applies Ottawa Ankle Rules to decide on X-ray given the gardening/injury history
eTG-aligned acute gout treatment (NSAID OR colchicine OR short oral prednisolone by renal function); reviews thiazide and plans allopurinol to target urate once settled if indicated
Clear empathic lay explanation of gouty arthritis (uric-acid crystals) and the plan
Addresses pain, work impact and safety-netting/follow-up

red_flags: Acute hot, swollen, tender joint - treat as septic arthritis until aspiration excludes it; afebrile status does NOT exclude infection
Cellulitis with a skin break/entry point and spreading erythema (a common exam differential)
Constitutional symptoms (fever, weight loss, night sweats) suggesting infection or malignancy
Neurovascular compromise - pallor/claudication (PAD) or unilateral calf swelling with clotting risk (DVT)
australian_guidelines: eTG (Therapeutic Guidelines, Australia) - acute gout: NSAID (e.g. naproxen) OR low-dose colchicine OR a short course of oral prednisolone chosen by renal function and comorbidity

eTG - once the flare settles, urate-lowering therapy with allopurinol titrated to a target serum urate for recurrent attacks, tophi, urate stones or CKD; serum urate may be normal during an acute flare
Ottawa Ankle Rules - evidence-based decision rule to determine the need for ankle/foot X-ray after injury, reducing unnecessary imaging
PBS - allopurinol available for long-term urate-lowering therapy; review thiazide diuretics as a modifiable gout precipitant
learning_objectives: Apply a grouped foot/ankle differential framework (bone/joint, soft tissue, neurovascular, red flags, trauma) to acute ankle pain
Recognise that a normal temperature does not exclude septic arthritis and that joint aspiration precedes a gout diagnosis
Identify thiazide diuretics and dietary triggers as gout risk factors and that gout is not limited to the great toe
Select eTG-aligned acute and preventive gout management and apply the Ottawa Ankle Rules for imaging decisions
key_points: Definitive gout = negatively birefringent monosodium urate crystals on polarised microscopy; joint aspiration also excludes sepsis
Hydrochlorothiazide raises serum urate and precipitates gout - a high-yield OSCE clue
Preferred terminology is 'Achilles tendinopathy' (degeneration, little true inflammation); use the Simmonds-Thompson calf-squeeze test to exclude rupture
Ottawa Ankle Rules guide the need for X-ray after the gardening/injury history and reduce unnecessary imaging

citations.claim: The case's structured ankle differential (traumatic sprains/Achilles rupture; infective pyogenic arthritis; inflammatory RA; degenerative OA; tenosynovitis) is supported by a dedicated ankle-causes list, including joint aspiration for Gram stain/culture and microscopy for crystals.
Gout characteristically involves the great toe but can affect the ankle, knee and other joints and is prone to recurrence, supporting the teaching that 'gout is not only in the big toe'.

Osteoarthritis features (hard/bony swelling, crepitus, mild inflammatory signs, restricted movement, pain worse by end of day, relieved by rest, no systemic manifestations) support distinguishing hallux rigidus/OA from crystal/inflammatory arthropathy.
